claim: The nervous system of Caenorhabditis elegans has 302 neurons and 56 glia.
source: apart from the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans (302 neurons, 56 glia) (White et al., 1986)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to White et al., 1986.

claim: The exact numbers of cells within the central nervous system of model organisms or humans is currently unknown.
source: the exact numbers of cells within the central nervous system (CNS) of model organisms or that of humans is currently unknown, with estimates, including those based on extrapolation from direct quantification of brain sub-regions, varying widely (Silbereis et al., 2016; Keller et al., 2018; von Bartheld et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple sources discussing the variability of estimates.

claim: A range of 10,000–15,000 active neurons has been proposed for the larval Drosophila CNS.
source: For the larval CNS, a range of 10,000–15,000 active neurons has been proposed (Scott et al., 2001; Meinertzhagen, 2018; Eschbach and Zlatic, 2020) across developmental time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Scott et al., 2001; Meinertzhagen, 2018; Eschbach and Zlatic, 2020.

claim: For adult Drosophila, approximations have been suggested in the range of 100,000–199,000 neurons in the brain.
source: For adult Drosophila, approximations have been suggested in the range of 100,000–199,000 neurons in the brain (Simpson, 2009; Chiang et al., 2011; Kaiser, 2015; Scheffer and Meinertzhagen, 2019; Raji and Potter, 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple sources.

claim: The adult Drosophila VNC has a range of 10,000–20,000 cells.
source: together with a range of 10,000–20,000 cells in the VNC (Birkholz et al., 2015; Lacin et al., 2019; Bates et al., 2019; Allen et al., 2020)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Birkholz et al., 2015; Lacin et al., 2019; Bates et al., 2019; Allen et al., 2020.

claim: Glia has been estimated to be approximately 10% of the number of neurons in Drosophila.
source: The other major CNS cell type, glia, has been estimated to be approximately 10% of the number of neurons (Kremer et al., 2017; Meinertzhagen, 2018; Raji and Potter, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kremer et al., 2017; Meinertzhagen, 2018; Raji and Potter, 2021.

claim: Immature neurons within the larval CNS are unlikely to contribute to larval CNS function.
source: These immature neurons are unlikely to contribute to larval CNS function and are generally excluded when considering larval neuronal circuit architecture (Eichler et al., 2017; Scheffer and Meinertzhagen, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eichler et al., 2017; Scheffer and Meinertzhagen, 2019.

claim: Only a small fraction of the total number of larval CNS cells may actually contribute to CNS function.
source: It has been suggested that only a small fraction of the total number of larval CNS cells may actually contribute to CNS function (Ravenscroft et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ravenscroft et al., 2020.

claim: The female third instar larval CNS had 10,312 ±5.03%, n=16, neurons.
source: Averaging across the lines, we found that the female third instar larval CNS had 10,312 ±5.03%, n=16, neurons (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification of neurons in female larvae.

claim: The female Drosophila larval CNS had 3860 ±3.37%, n=7, glia.
source: We measured 3860 ±3.37%, n=7, glia in the female CNS (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification of glia in female larvae.

claim: The number of glia in the female larval CNS amounted to 37% of the number of neurons.
source: This amounted to 37% of the number of neurons, far more than previously estimated (Meinertzhagen, 2018; Raji and Potter, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to previous estimates cited.

claim: The male third instar larval CNS had 9396 ±5.59%, n=15 neurons.
source: Averaging across the lines, we found that the male third instar larval CNS had 9396 ±5.59%, n=15 neurons, significantly fewer than those of females (–9.75%, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification of neurons in male larvae.

claim: Males have significantly fewer CNS neurons than females.
source: Averaging across the lines, we found that the male third instar larval CNS had 9396 ±5.59%, n=15 neurons, significantly fewer than those of females (–9.75%, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing statistical significance.

claim: Males had 4015 ±1.98%, n=6, glia.
source: We found that males had 4015 ±1.98%, n=6, glia far more than previous estimates (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification of glia in male larvae.

claim: The number of glia in the male larval CNS was significantly more than in females.
source: The number of glia in the male larval CNS was significantly more than in females (+3.86%, p=0.0284).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing statistical significance.

claim: Male Drosophila larva have significantly fewer CNS neurons than females but more glia.
source: In summary, male Drosophila larva have significantly fewer CNS neurons than females but more glia.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bruchpilot is a critical presynaptic active zone component widely used to label Drosophila synapses.
source: Bruchpilot (Brp) is a critical presynaptic active zone component widely used to label Drosophila synapses, including for large-scale circuit analyses (Wagh et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wagh et al., 2006.

claim: The brp-GAL4 line labeled 10,776 (±2.65%, n=6) neurons in the female CNS.
source: We found that the CNS labelled by brp-GAL4 had 10,776 (±2.65%, n=6) neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification.

claim: The Syt1-GAL4 line labeled 10,097 (±5.96%, n=5) neurons in the female CNS.
source: Syt1-GAL4 had 10,097 (±5.96%, n=5) neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification.

claim: The nSyb-GAL4 line labeled 9971 (±1.35%, n=5) neurons in the female CNS.
source: nSyb-GAL4 had 9971 (±1.35%, n=5) neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification.

claim: brp-GAL4 labeled significantly more neurons than either Syt1 or nSyb GAL4 lines in females.
source: We tested the statistical difference in the numbers of neurons labelled by these lines and found that while nSyb-GAL4 and Syt1-GAL4 were not statistically different from each other, brp-GAL4 did label significantly more neurons than either Syt1 or nSyb GAL4 lines (brp-GAL4 vs Syt1-GAL4+6.72%, p=0.03, brp-GAL4 vs nSyb-GAL4 +8.07%, p=0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing statistical significance.

claim: The brp, Syt1 and nSyb GAL4 lines label only neurons and not glial cells.
source: We found complete exclusion of cells labelled by brp, Syt1 and nSyb GAL4 lines from cells labelled by repo (Figure 2d, brp-GAL4 & repo-QF2 Video 7, Syt1-GAL4 & repo-QF2 Video 8, nSyb-GAL4 & repo-QF2 Video 9), consistent with the brp, Syt1 and nSyb GAL4 lines labelling only neurons that express synaptic protein genes and not glial cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing complete exclusion of labeling between neuronal and glial markers.

claim: The inter-nuclei distance of glial cell nuclei exhibited a unimodal distribution.
source: Using this measurement, we found that the inter-nuclei distance of glial cell nuclei exhibited a unimodal distribution (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: All three neuronal lines exhibited a bimodal distribution of inter-nuclei distances.
source: In contrast, all three neuronal lines exhibited a bimodal distribution of inter-nuclei distances (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: brp-GAL4 labeled 9888 (±3.15%, n=5) neurons in males.
source: We found that brp-GAL4 labelled 9888 (±3.15%, n=5) neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification in male larvae.

claim: Syt1-GAL4 labeled 9012 (±3.8%, n=5) neurons in males.
source: Syt1-GAL4 labelled 9012 (±3.8%, n=5) neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification in male larvae.

claim: nSyb-GAL4 labeled 9286 (±5.38%, n=5) neurons in male larvae.
source: nSyb-GAL4 labelled 9286 (±5.38%, n=5) neurons in male larvae
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification in male larvae.

claim: Topological analysis supports that sexual dimorphism extends to deeper features of CNS organisation.
source: Utilisation of these topological summaries in a support vector machine also supports that sexual dimorphism extends to deeper features of CNS organisation.
evidence: The claim is supported by topological data analysis and machine learning results.

claim: The SVM is able to extract the sex of the animal reliably from topological features.
source: The distribution of these correlations (Figure 3f), exhibiting clearly that the SVM is able to extract the sex of the animal reliably: only about 1.9% of the splits result in a higher correlation in the control set than in the true data.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3f demonstrating SVM performance.

claim: Simpler point cloud features like properties of the distributions of inter-nuclei distances did not produce a significant signal for sex classification.
source: Moreover, repeating the procedure with simpler point cloud features, like properties of the distributions of inter-nuclei distances, did not produce a significant signal (Figure 3g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Sh was expressed in 8204 ±5.67%, n=10 neurons in males.
source: We found that Sh and Shal were expressed in large numbers of neurons 8204 ±5.67%, n=10 and 8261 ±3.1%, n=5 respectively
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification of Sh expression.

claim: Shal was expressed in 8261 ±3.1%, n=5 neurons in males.
source: We found that Sh and Shal were expressed in large numbers of neurons 8204 ±5.67%, n=10 and 8261 ±3.1%, n=5 respectively
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification of Shal expression.

claim: Sh and Shal were expressed in significantly less neurons than the average number of all male neurons.
source: We found that Sh and Shal were expressed in large numbers of neurons 8204 ±5.67%, n=10 and 8261 ±3.1%, n=5 respectively, though significantly less (–12.7% and −12.1%, p<0.0001) than the average number of all male neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing statistical significance.

claim: Shab was expressed in 3057 ±8.21%, n=10 neurons in males.
source: In contrast, Shab (3057 ±8.21%, n=10) and Shaw (1737 ±4.3%, n=11) were expressed in smaller numbers of neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification of Shab expression.

claim: Shaw was expressed in 1737 ±4.3%, n=11 neurons in males.
source: In contrast, Shab (3057 ±8.21%, n=10) and Shaw (1737 ±4.3%, n=11) were expressed in smaller numbers of neurons
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from quantification of Shaw expression.

claim: Shab was expressed in only 32.5% of total male neurons.
source: with expression observed in only 32.5% or 18.5% of total male neurons respectively
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data calculating the percentage of neurons expressing Shab.

claim: Shaw was expressed in only 18.5% of total male neurons.
source: with expression observed in only 32.5% or 18.5% of total male neurons respectively
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data calculating the percentage of neurons expressing Shaw.

claim: Shab and Shaw had very reduced expression in the brain lobes of larva compared with Sh and Shal.
source: In particular, Shab and Shaw had very reduced expression in the brain lobes of larva (Figure 4c and d) compared with Sh and Shal (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: All four potassium channel GAL4 lines express in motor neurons.
source: All four lines express in motor neurons as predicted from mutant analysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The brp, Syt1 and nSyb GAL4 lines were not expressed prior to embryonic stage 16.
source: We detected no expression from any of the three lines prior to embryonic stage 16 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: Beginning at stage 17 of embryonic development, all three lines displayed expression in both the CNS and peripheral nervous system.
source: However, beginning at stage 17 of embryonic development, when synaptic activity begins (Baines and Bate, 1998), all three lines displayed expression in both the CNS and peripheral nervous system (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and a citation to Baines and Bate, 1998.

claim: Labelling by all three lines did not overlap with Deadpan expression.
source: We found that labelling by all three lines did not overlap with Deadpan expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), suggesting these lines are not expressed in neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The three neuronal lines are not expressed in neuroblasts.
source: We found that labelling by all three lines did not overlap with Deadpan expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), suggesting these lines are not expressed in neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of overlap with Deadpan, a neuroblast marker.

claim: All three lines labeled a large fraction but not all of the total cells in the adult brain.
source: We also examined expression of all three lines in the adult brain and, as in the larval CNS, observed labelling of a large fraction but not all of the total cells in the adult brain (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Manual and automated quantification of nuclei numbers in dopaminergic, serotonergic, and dopa decarboxylase expressing neurons are similar.
source: (h) Manual or automated quantification of nuclei numbers in these volumes are similar.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1h comparing manual and automated counts.

claim: The automated count of a brp-GAL4 labelled CNS differed from manual count by just 14 neurons.
source: Similar to our experiments with sparse neuronal labelling, we found good agreement between manual and automated quantification with a difference of just 14 neurons (9430 nuclei manual vs 9444 nuclei automated for this individual CNS).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing manual and automated quantification.

claim: The female Drosophila larval CNS had 10,312 neurons, fewer than most previous predictions.
source: In sum, we found that the female Drosophila larval CNS had 10,312 neurons, fewer than most previous predictions, and several fold more glia than previously thought.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to previous estimates.

claim: The female Drosophila larval CNS had several fold more glia than previously thought.
source: In sum, we found that the female Drosophila larval CNS had 10,312 neurons, fewer than most previous predictions, and several fold more glia than previously thought.

source: However, beginning at stage 17 of embryonic development, when synaptic activity begins (Baines and Bate, 1998)

claim: Repo is a glial specific transcription factor.
source: we compared their expression to that of glial cells labelled by glial specific transcription factor Repo (Xiong et al., 1994; Lin and Potter, 2016)

claim: Synaptotagmin 1 is the fast calcium sensor for synaptic neurotransmitter release.
source: which encodes Synaptotagmin 1 (Littleton et al., 1994), the fast calcium sensor for synaptic neurotransmitter release (Quiñones-Frías and Littleton, 2021)

claim: neuronal Synaptobrevin encodes an essential presynaptic vSNARE.
source: which encodes an essential presynaptic vSNARE (Südhof and Rothman, 2009)

claim: The large relative ratio of glia observed in the third instar larva could conceivably be glia produced in advance of adult CNS development.
source: An important potential caveat, however, is that the large relative ratio of glia we observe in the third instar larva could conceivably be glia produced in advance of adult CNS development.

source: As adult specific neuron numbers expand during pupation, the relative ratio of glia could potentially decline.

claim: The Drosophila CNS is comprised of both a brain and ventral nerve cord.
source: Nonetheless, the precise number of cells (neurons or glia) in either the smaller larval or larger adult Drosophila CNS, comprised of both a brain and ventral nerve cord (VNC), remain unknown

claim: Encompassed within and surrounding the larval CNS are dividing neuroblasts, which will give rise to adult neurons.
source: First, encompassed within and surrounding the larval CNS are dividing neuroblasts, which will give rise to adult neurons (Doe, 2017).

claim: Human females have more olfactory bulb neurons and glia than males.
source: and human females have also been reported to have more olfactory bulb neurons and glia than males (Oliveira-Pinto et al., 2014).

claim: Few sexually dimorphic behavioural differences have been reported in Drosophila larva.

claim: The glial-neuron ratios for rodents or rabbits are similar to the 0.4 ratio found in larval Drosophila CNS.
source: In the larval Drosophila CNS, we found closer to 0.4 glial cells per neuron on average, more similar to the glial-neuron ratios reported for rodents or rabbits (Verkhratsky and Butt, 2018).

claim: Stereological counting of subregions assumes homogenous cell density across the organ or within subregions.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to von Bartheld et al., 2016; Keller et al., 2018.
